thread.title: How Apple Is Changing Course In India - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Steve Brodrick
title: How Apple Is Changing Course In India - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Apple's Opportunity In Tim Cook's recent letter to shareholders January 2, 2019, the Apple Inc. ( AAPL ) CEO spoke about the current challenges the company is facing in emerging markets. In this letter, he mentioned China eleven times but did not mention India once. In Q3 2018, shipments of smartphones in India surpassed those of the U.S. over the quarter. This is now the second time that U.S. sales have slipped behind India, cementing India as the second-largest smartphone market in the world after China. Despite topping 400 million smartphone users in June 2018, the Indian market remains relatively under-penetrated. By all indications, India has more room to grow.
With iPhone unit replacement rates slowing down in the developed world and the smartphone market saturated, the future of the smartphone market is in the emerging economies of the developing world. Not only are market penetration rates low in developing countries, population growth rates are high and per capita income is increasing at a rapid pace. With Apple's problems piling up in China, it cannot afford to squander its tremendous opportunity in the Indian smartphone market.
The Importance of iPhone to Apple The iPhone is one of the most successful consumer products of all time. Its massive success has swelled the portion of revenue attributable to this one product to an outsized portion of Apple’s total revenue mix. This has caused the company’s quarterly results to be hyper-dependent on iPhone sales. In the fourth quarter of 2018, Apple generated 59.12% of its revenue from iPhone sales . The proportion of revenue derived from the iPhone is down from the Q1 2018 high of 69.74% due to growth in some of Apple's other product lines. However, the percentage of the company's revenue derived from its flagship product has not been less than 50% since the fourth quarter of 2012. Unfortunately for Apple, the product that enabled its dominance in North America with a 52.43% market share in the smartphone market has not garnered the same success globally. As of December 2018, Apple's global market share was 13.2%, compared to Samsung's ( OTC:SSNLF ) 20.3%. This more modest market share reflects the iPhone's struggle for widespread adoption in emerging markets.
With replacement cycles for smartphones elongating in developed markets and new iterations of iPhones only adding marginal improvements, there is little visibility for growth in the smartphone markets of developed economies. These trends, coupled with market saturation and high penetration rates in the developed world, suggest that Apple's future revenues rely on the company acquiring new consumers. By necessity, this growth needs to come from the developing world, where populations are growing and a new middle class is emerging with an appetite for the latest consumer goods.
(Source: Cult of Mac )
The India n Smartphone Market According to The Economist , the number of internet users in India was just 125 million three years ago. By November 2018, that number had more than tripled to 512 million connections. Today, India adds approximately 16 million new internet connection per month, almost all of them on mobile phones. On top of this rapid growth in connectivity, Indians are also prolific users of mobile data. In 2017, the average Indian mobile phone user consumed 4.13 GB/month , compared to the Organization of Economic Development (OECD) average of 2.8 GB/month . This rapid growth in connected users and eager adoption of smartphones makes India a very attractive market for manufacturers of smartphones and other connected devices.
For Q3 2018, Counterpoint Research reported that the smartphone segment contributed to half of the total handset market in the most recent quarter. In the same quarter, India’s smartphone shipments reached a new record of 42.6 million units - an increase of 9.1% over the same period in 2017 . Current estimates suggest that only 24% of India's 1.3 billion citizens own a smartphone, suggesting that the country's market has a current potential for an additional 1.04 billion smartphones to reach the OECD smartphone penetration average of 102%. In addition to India's ample room to run with smartphone market penetration, it also has a population that is still growing. In 2017, India's population growth rate was 1.1%, well ahead of China's 0.6% or the United States' 0.7% growth rates .
The Indian smartphone market is dominated by five brands that account for a 77% share of the total smartphone market. Over the past few years, the market has been steadily consolidating as the largest five producers led by Xiaomi ( XI ) and Samsung capture more market share. Notably absent from the top five brands in India is Apple, which shipped fewer than 1 million iPhones in India in the first half of 2018. While globally Apple is a top three smartphone manufacturer, in India the iPhone represented less than 2% of the 60 million smartphones that were shipped in the country during that period. For context, over the same period, Samsung and Xiaomi shipped 17.4 million and 19 million smartphones respectively to Indian consumers.
(Source: Dazeinfo DGraph/ Data Source: Counterpoint Research )
Sales Strategy In the summer of 2018, three of Apple's top executives in India left the company amid disappointing sales growth. Apple's new head of country, Michel Coulomb, is reversing the sales strategy of his predecessor Sanjay Kaul and moving to a system of controlled distribution. Apple's previous strategy of open distribution gave significant control to re-sellers who offered iPhone products at discounted rates and offered non-standard pricing across the county.
India is a highly fractured market for smartphone sales, characterized by high decentralization and small local vendors. iPhone pricing in India has been somewhat heterogeneous as some retailers change prices or offer discounts arbitrarily. Apple's new leadership in the country has made an effort to control pricing more directly by offering training to retail staff and by offering all year-round deals to reduce and standardize prices. The company has also indicated that it will cut inventory shipments to retailers who fail to hit sales targets, to prioritize iPhone recommendations from sales staff. In 2018, Apple was successful in expanding the number of physical third-party stores that carry the iPhone.
Due to the lack of control Apple has had in the Indian retail environment and the roadblocks it has encountered in the opening of its own stores, the firm has become over-reliant on online sales in India. In May 2017, the Economic Times reported that 50-55% of iPhone sales in India were online, compared to the industry average of 30%. Apple is pursuing plans to open flagship retail outlets in New Delhi, Bengaluru and Mumbai. The company has long attempted to open retail stores in India but has not been able to meet the government regulations to do so. One of these barriers is a requirement to manufacture a minimum of 30% of its products in the country. With plans to start making the iPhone 6s in country, along with using more local suppliers, it is finally on track to opening these retail locations.
(Source: Economic Times )
Pricing Strategy According to Zacks Investment Research , Apple’s Q3 2018 iPhone revenue soared 20% to $29.91 billion from $24.8 billion over the same period in 2017. Despite this impressive revenue growth, iPhone unit sales only increased 0.7% to 41.30 million in Q3 2018, up from 41.02 million in Q3 2017. The significant difference between total unit sale growth and total revenue growth highlights that Apple's revenue has been dependent on the high-priced iPhone X. This suggests that the company's strategy is less concerned with volume growth than it is with margin and premium pricing. While premium pricing seems to have been effective for revenue growth in developed markets, this reliance on premium pricing has not translated to the same success in developing markets like India.
The company has been struggling to gain market share in India as it attempts to compete in the mid-range and premium smartphone markets. While India's premium smartphone market ($500+ models) close to doubled from Q2 2017 to Q2 2018, Apple continues to lose ground to Samsung in this space. From Q1 2017, to Q1 2018, its share of the premium market dipped from 45% to approximately 20% as it was displaced by continued strong shipments of Samsung Galaxy S9 series and OnePlus 6, which have now surpassed the iPhone, relegating Apple to third place in the premium end of the market.
(Source: Cult of Mac )
As of the first quarter of 2018, the premium smartphone market only represents 4% of the overall market in India. However, the mid-end smartphone segment (Rs 15,000-20,000 range), a segment that expanded 158% in the first quarter of 2017, continues to be the fastest-growing in India. The growing availability of financing options by retailers has resulted in an increase in the average selling price for smartphones. The average selling price rose to a record high of $167 (~Rs 11,620) in the second quarter of 2018, up from $157 (~Rs 10,924) in April-June 2017. Despite the growth in the mid-end segment and a rising average selling price, the iPhone still seems to be on the expensive side of a price-sensitive market. In May 2017, Forbes reported that Apple planned to cut prices for its 2013 iPhone 5S model in the Indian market from $280 to around $230 in an effort to respond to consumer price sensitivity.
With the introduction of the iPhone X, Apple seems to have doubled down on its premium pricing strategy at the global level. With many cheaper models in the market, the company's pricing strategy does not appear to be working in India. The lack of sales traction in India points to the need for a cheaper iPhone to help Apple carve out its market niche. Even older models such as the iPhone SE and iPhone 6S, costing $430 and $270 respectively, are not affordable for the average Indian consumer. Shifting more manufacturing to India will help bring down costs, but ultimately, Apple should consider developing a new product specifically for developing markets. The company can't afford to wait the years it will take for India's consumers to grow their disposal income to the point where they can afford to purchase iPhones at U.S. prices. In order for Apple to succeed in India, it needs to grow market share before the market matures and consumers form strong brand loyalties with other providers.
As iPhone users tend to be very loyal, Apple often needs only to sell the first device to an individual to gain a potential customer for life. According to survey data compiled by Fluent, a U.S. marketing firm, 80% of iPhone users reported that they planned to stay loyal to Apple, while 70% stated that they would not even consider another brand. In the same survey, 41% of users of the iOS ecosystem cite that it would be too painful to consider switching. Users of the iPhone also experience strong benefits when pairing their Apple phone with the company's other products, including iPads and Apple Watches. This internal network effect helps Apple to earn other recurring revenue through apps and media sales. Given that iPhone users are unlikely to switch from Apple products or from the iOS ecosystem to other brands, that helps to insulate Apple from pricing sensitivity for subsequent smartphone purchases.
(Source: Bloomberg )
Indian Consumer Behavior Part of Apple's struggle in India has been a failure to understand local consumer behavior. Aside from a high degree of price sensitivity, Indian consumers of smartphones are highly influenced by technical dimensions of devices. According to Kunal Dua of The Verge , Indian users place a greater emphasis on technical dimensions such as the amount of RAM a smartphone has, or whether or not it offers a dual sim option for storage expansion. This preference set differs from that of American consumers, who tend to value the user experience over a product's spec sheet.
Another challenge that Apple has had in India is that it has not been able to offer iPhone users the full range of experience that many Western consumers are accustomed to. For instance, Siri has improved its understanding of Indian accents, however, the experience falls short of Siri's usability in other markets; or its competitor’s better-adapted language apps. The unavailability of Apple Pay is another example of the second-tier user experience that iPhone users have in India. While Samsung Pay has been available in India since March 2017, Apple Insider reports that Apple Pay will not be available in the country anytime soon, as it faces challenges over data storage and authentication rules.
In January 2019, Apple finally launched a new iteration of Apple Maps that supports directional navigational services. The company had been challenged to offer users a navigation tool for India's complicated road systems. This new map functionality also supports ride-sharing apps Uber ( UBER ) and Ola, which users previously had to access outside of Apple Maps. Although this service is not perfect, its long-awaited introduction will enhance the usability and value of the iPhone in the Indian market.
Apple users benefit from a network effect that does not seem to have found a critical mass in India. For example, functionality such as the availability of movie times and restaurant information that is commonplace in other markets is absent for Indian iPhone users. Part of the reason for this is that there are relatively few users of iPhone in India, thus there is not the same demand for app creation and specialization of the iPhone user experience in the country. As Apple builds a larger base of total iPhone users in India, the company should be able to grow momentum in offering an enhanced customer experience, even if the market share stays relatively low.
A Made in India Problem According to Reuters , Apple will begin assembling its top-end iPhones in India through Taiwanese manufacturer Foxconn ( OTC:FXCOF ) in early 2019. Foxconn will begin assembly of these higher-end iPhones at a plant in Tamil Nadu in southern India. This announcement made in late December 2018 is a good sign that Apple is paying attention to the vastly important Indian market. Although this move may be an effort to mitigate the potential risks of the U.S.-China trade war, the shift of focus from China to India is likely to achieve much more. Similarly, Apple production partner Wistron ( OTC:WICOF ) announced in January 2019 that it is investing $340 million in its Indian production facilities where it currently assembles iPhone SE and iPhone 6. These production announcements are developments that the Indian government has long awaited.
In September 2014, India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced the centerpiece of his administration's economic policy, the " Make in India " program. This initiative has a goal of transforming India into a global manufacturing hub, with a target of increasing the country's share of GDP attributable to manufacturing from 16% to 25% by 2022. The assembly of iPhones at this Foxconn factory in India is estimated to create an additional 25,000 jobs in the region. With the goal of creating 100 million jobs by 2022 through the "Make in India" program in the backdrop, Apple’s decision to relocate this plant is a gesture that is certain to endear the company to the country's government.
Caption: Apple CEO Tim Cook with India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi
(Source: Apple Insider )
India charges an import tax on handset components and finished devices imported into its consumer market. In February 2018, India increased the customs duty on imported mobile phones from 15% to 20% in an effort to protect local manufacturing. It is therefore unsurprising that around 75% of all cellphones sold in India last year were assembled in the country. As Apple currently imports almost 90% of the products it sells in India, the tariffs on imported phones create a significant cost disadvantage. The shift to manufacture some iPhones in the country will help reduce prices - savings that Apple can then pass on to the Indian consumer. This pricing advantage is essential for the company's success in the subcontinent, as price strategy is a key determinant of market share in developing economies.
Investor Takeaways Apple is currently trading at a modest P/E ratio of ~13.2, well down from its 5-year average of 15.4. Similarly, its current price/sales ratio is 3.0, down 10% from the long-term average of 3.3. This multiple contraction reflects the slowing of the company's growth. For Apple to maintain its current multiple, it will need to demonstrate to investors that it can still grow. The company's valuation will remain muted or continue to contract if there is no obvious path to market share growth in the developing world.
Apple's key to gaining a foothold in India is the expansion of local manufacturing. Enlarging a local manufacturing presence will enable it to lower prices and to build Apple Stores facilitating the expansion of the company’s retail network. Over the longer term, Apple will need to develop a less expensive iPhone that meets the needs of Indian consumers. Over the last six months, the company has made positive steps in India, including learning more about Indian consumers and replacing management and sales strategy. Despite these efforts, Apple has a lot of catching up to do with its competitors in India. Investors need to see the company demonstrate that it still has the ability to achieve growth. If Apple can turn things around in India, it would be a strong indicator that the company can apply some of the same sales strategies in other developing economies. With China's growth slowing and the domestic U.S. market saturated, Apple can't afford to fail in the world's second-largest smartphone market.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours.
